cards.prompt: A purified collected H2O sample has mass 65.0 g. Define actual yield, report it in grams and moles using 18.015 g/mol with appropriate significant figures, state what measurement information should accompany it, and explain why an apparent actual yield can exceed theoretical yield.
required_concepts: Define actual yield as experimentally measured or isolated product under a stated procedure and basis.
Report 65.0 g H2O and convert it to 3.61 mol H2O using 18.015 g/mol and three significant figures.
Require product identity, units, measurement precision or uncertainty, and a stated collection and purity basis for an interpretable report.
Explain that apparent actual yield above theoretical yield is diagnostic of contamination, retained solvent, error, or inconsistent accounting.

accepted_variants: Percent yield is 100 times the ratio of actual to theoretical yield.
65.0 g divided by 72.1 g gives a 90.2 percent yield.
The experiment recovered 90.2% of the stoichiometric theoretical amount.
cards.definition: **Percent yield** compares measured product with the nonzero theoretical benchmark: percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%. The numerator and denominator must refer to the same product and use compatible units. For 65.0 g actual and 72.1 g theoretical, (65.0/72.1) × 100% = 90.2% to three significant figures. The ratio is dimensionless but reported as a percent; its precision cannot exceed that justified by the input measurements. A result above 100% normally indicates impurities, retained solvent, measurement error, or inconsistent product or unit bases and should be investigated.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the ratio and dividing theoretical yield by actual yield.
Dividing amounts for different products or mixing incompatible units without conversion.
Rounding 90.152... to an unjustified precision or treating a yield above 100% as automatically valid.
cards.prompt: Define percent yield and calculate it for an actual yield of 65.0 g H2O and a theoretical yield of 72.1 g H2O. State the unit convention, significant figures, uncertainty boundary, and interpretation of a result above 100%.
required_concepts: State percent yield = actual yield divided by nonzero theoretical yield times 100 percent.
Require the same product and compatible amount units in numerator and denominator.
Calculate 90.2% from 65.0 g / 72.1 g and report three significant figures.
Treat a value above 100% as a diagnostic for contamination, error, or inconsistent accounting rather than automatically accepting it.

accepted_variants: Electromagnetic radiation is propagating oscillation of electric and magnetic fields that carries energy and momentum.
Light can be described as a wave with wavelength and frequency or as photons with quantized energy.
Electromagnetic waves need no material medium and travel at the vacuum speed c only in vacuum.
cards.definition: **Electromagnetic radiation** is energy and momentum propagated by coupled oscillating electric and magnetic fields. Its wave description uses wavelength λ, frequency ν, and speed v; its quantum description assigns energy hν and momentum to photons. Visible light is one band of the electromagnetic spectrum, alongside radio, infrared, ultraviolet, X rays, and gamma rays. Unlike a mechanical wave, electromagnetic radiation does not require a material medium and travels at c in vacuum. In matter it usually propagates more slowly and interacts with atoms or molecules, so the vacuum relation must not be applied as though every medium had speed c.
major_error_concepts: Claiming that light requires air or another material medium in order to propagate.
Treating the wave and photon descriptions as mutually exclusive alternatives rather than complementary models.
Claiming that electromagnetic radiation travels at exactly c in every material.
cards.prompt: Define electromagnetic radiation using both wave and photon descriptions, give visible light as an example, contrast it with a mechanical wave, and state how its propagation speed differs in vacuum and matter.
required_concepts: Describe electromagnetic radiation as coupled electric and magnetic field propagation carrying energy and momentum.
Connect the wave variables λ, ν, and v with the photon energy hν.
Identify visible light as one part of a broader electromagnetic spectrum and contrast electromagnetic waves with mechanical waves that require matter.
State that propagation is at c in vacuum but generally slower and medium-dependent in matter.

accepted_variants: Wavelength is the spatial period or crest-to-crest distance of a wave.
Four wavelengths span the first-to-fifth crest distance, so λ is 0.500 micrometers or 5.00 × 10^2 nanometers.
At fixed propagation speed, longer wavelength corresponds to lower frequency.
cards.definition: **Wavelength** λ is the spatial period of a wave: the distance, measured along propagation, between successive equal-phase points such as adjacent crests. From the first to the fifth crest there are four crest-to-crest intervals, so λ = 2.00 μm / 4 = 0.500 μm = 5.00 × 10^-7 m = 5.00 × 10^2 nm; the counted 4 is exact and the measured 2.00 μm fixes three significant figures. For a wave, v = λν. Wavelength is a distance, not a time rate, and it can change when radiation enters a new medium because speed changes while source-set frequency is normally preserved.
major_error_concepts: Dividing 2.00 μm by five crests rather than by the four intervals between them.
Converting 0.500 μm to 5.00 × 10^-4 m instead of 5.00 × 10^-7 m.
Defining wavelength as cycles per second or claiming it never changes between media.
cards.prompt: Define wavelength. If the distance from the first to the fifth successive crest of visible radiation is 2.00 μm, calculate λ in μm, meters, and nanometers with justified significant figures; then state its relation to speed and frequency and its medium boundary.
required_concepts: Define wavelength as the spatial distance between successive equal-phase points and give λ a length unit.
Recognize four intervals from the first through fifth crest and calculate 0.500 μm = 5.00 × 10^-7 m = 5.00 × 10^2 nm.
State v = λν and the inverse wavelength-frequency relation at fixed speed.
Report three significant figures and state that wavelength may change across media even when frequency remains fixed.

accepted_variants: Frequency is the number of wave cycles passing per second.
The radiation has frequency 6.00 × 10^14 Hz.
At fixed speed, higher frequency means shorter wavelength.
cards.definition: **Frequency** ν is the number of complete oscillation cycles per unit time, measured in s^-1 or hertz (Hz). For 3.00 × 10^15 cycles in 5.00 s, ν = cycles/time = 6.00 × 10^14 s^-1 = 6.00 × 10^14 Hz, reported to three significant figures. The wave relation is v = λν, so at fixed speed frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength. Frequency is set by the source and normally remains unchanged when radiation crosses a stationary medium boundary; speed and wavelength change instead.
major_error_concepts: Reporting frequency in meters or nanometers rather than inverse seconds.
Multiplying cycles by time and obtaining 1.50 × 10^16 Hz.
Claiming that frequency must decrease whenever light enters a slower medium.
cards.prompt: Define frequency. Radiation completes 3.00 × 10^15 cycles in 5.00 s; calculate ν in hertz with justified significant figures, relate frequency to wavelength and speed, and state what normally happens to frequency at a medium boundary.
required_concepts: Define frequency as cycles per unit time with units s^-1 or Hz.
Calculate 6.00 × 10^14 Hz from 3.00 × 10^15 cycles divided by 5.00 s and retain three significant figures.
Relate frequency to wavelength and propagation speed through v = λν.
State that frequency normally remains fixed across a stationary medium boundary while speed and wavelength adjust.

accepted_variants: The exact vacuum light speed is 299792458 meters per second.
Multiplying 500.0 nm by 5.996 × 10^14 Hz gives 2.998 × 10^8 m/s.
Electromagnetic radiation travels at c in vacuum and generally at c divided by refractive index in a material.
cards.definition: The **speed of light in vacuum**, c, is exactly 299,792,458 m/s. Any wave satisfies v = λν; for λ = 500.0 nm = 5.000 × 10^-7 m and ν = 5.996 × 10^14 s^-1, v = λν = 2.998 × 10^8 m/s to four significant figures, consistent with c within the rounded inputs. The exact definition of c has no measurement uncertainty, but a calculated value inherits the precision or uncertainty of λ and ν. In a material, phase speed is generally v = c/n rather than c, so c = λν applies specifically to vacuum wavelengths and frequencies.
major_error_concepts: Using 500.0 directly as meters without converting nanometers.
Adding λ and ν rather than multiplying them in v = λν.
Claiming that the exact vacuum value c is the propagation speed in every medium.
cards.prompt: State the exact vacuum speed of light and its units. For λ = 500.0 nm and ν = 5.996 × 10^14 Hz, calculate the propagation speed with justified significant figures, compare it with c, and state the material-medium boundary.
required_concepts: State c = 299,792,458 m/s exactly in vacuum.
Convert 500.0 nm to 5.000 × 10^-7 m and calculate 2.998 × 10^8 m/s from λν.
Distinguish the exact defined constant c from a calculated value limited by measured λ and ν.
State that propagation in a material generally has v = c/n and must not automatically be assigned the vacuum speed.

accepted_variants: Photon energy equals Planck's constant times frequency.
A 5.00 × 10^2 nm photon has energy 3.97 × 10^-19 joule.
The same 5.00 × 10^2 nm radiation corresponds to about 239 kilojoules per mole of photons.
cards.definition: A **photon's energy** is E = hν; in vacuum, using c = λν, the equivalent relation is E = hc/λ. For λ = 5.00 × 10^2 nm = 5.00 × 10^-7 m, E = (6.62607015 × 10^-34 J s)(299792458 m/s)/(5.00 × 10^-7 m) = 3.97 × 10^-19 J per photon to three significant figures. Multiplying by Avogadro's constant gives about 239 kJ/mol of photons. The constants h and c are exact in SI, so the wavelength controls the reported precision. Higher frequency or shorter wavelength means greater photon energy; energy per photon must not be confused with energy per mole.
major_error_concepts: Using E = h/ν instead of E = hν.
Substituting 500 into hc/λ without converting nanometers to meters.
Reporting 3.97 × 10^-19 J as a molar energy rather than the energy of one photon.
cards.prompt: Define photon energy and calculate the energy of one 5.00 × 10^2 nm photon using h = 6.62607015 × 10^-34 J s and c = 299792458 m/s. Give the equivalent E = hν relation, report justified significant figures, and distinguish one-photon from molar energy.
required_concepts: State E = hν and the vacuum equivalent E = hc/λ.
Convert 5.00 × 10^2 nm to 5.00 × 10^-7 m and calculate 3.97 × 10^-19 J per photon to three significant figures.
Relate higher frequency and shorter wavelength to larger photon energy.
Distinguish energy per photon from the approximately 239 kJ/mol molar photon energy.

accepted_variants: An atomic emission spectrum is a discrete set of wavelengths released when excited electrons fall to lower allowed levels.
Each emitted line has photon energy equal to the difference between the initial and final atomic energy levels.
Hydrogen emits its roughly 656 nm H-alpha line when an electron transitions from n = 3 to n = 2.
cards.definition: An **atomic emission spectrum** is the set of discrete wavelengths emitted by excited atoms as electrons make allowed transitions from higher to lower energy states. Each line satisfies Ephoton = Ehigh − Elow = hν = hc/λ. In atomic hydrogen, the approximately 656.3 nm H-alpha line is emitted in the n = 3 to n = 2 transition. The line pattern reflects quantized level spacings and can identify an element, unlike a continuous thermal spectrum. Emission is the downward-transition counterpart of absorption, but observed lines and intensities also depend on allowed-transition rules, state populations, environment, and instrument response; they are not determined by abundance alone.
major_error_concepts: Describing atomic emission as electrons absorbing photons to move upward in energy.
Claiming that an isolated atom produces an unrestricted continuous spectrum rather than characteristic lines.
Assuming every energy-level pair must yield an observed line or that line intensity measures abundance alone.
cards.prompt: Define an atomic emission spectrum, explain the electron transition and photon-energy relation that produces each line, use hydrogen's approximately 656.3 nm line as an example, contrast emission with absorption, and state why real spectra need not contain every possible transition or simple abundance-only intensities.
required_concepts: Define emission lines as discrete photons released in allowed higher-to-lower atomic energy transitions.
Relate a line to its positive photon-energy gap by Ephoton = Ehigh − Elow = hν = hc/λ.
Use hydrogen's approximately 656.3 nm n = 3 to n = 2 line as a concrete example and contrast a line spectrum with a continuum.
Contrast emission with absorption and state that transition rules, populations, environment, and instrumentation affect observed lines and intensities.

accepted_variants: An atomic absorption spectrum contains discrete wavelengths absorbed when electrons move to higher allowed energy levels.
A dark absorption line occurs when incident photon energy matches an allowed gap from a populated lower state.
Sodium atoms can remove radiation near 589 nanometers through an electronic excitation.
cards.definition: An **atomic absorption spectrum** records discrete wavelengths removed from incident radiation when atoms absorb photons that drive allowed transitions from populated lower states to higher states. Absorption requires hν = hc/λ = Ehigh − Elow; a sodium atom can absorb near 589 nm when a photon matches an allowed electronic energy gap. The transmitted spectrum then has reduced intensity at that wavelength. Absorption raises electronic energy, whereas emission releases a photon in a downward transition. A potential level difference does not guarantee a visible line: the lower state must be populated, the transition must be allowed, and broadening, environment, and instrument response affect the observed feature.
major_error_concepts: Describing absorption as an electron falling and releasing a photon.
Claiming that any photon energy is absorbed continuously by an isolated atom.
Assuming an absorption spectrum must be a perfect inverse of emission regardless of state populations and selection rules.
cards.prompt: Define an atomic absorption spectrum, explain the transition and photon-energy condition for a dark line, use a sodium atom absorbing near 589 nm as an example, contrast absorption with emission, and state the population and allowed-transition boundary.
required_concepts: Define absorption lines as discrete incident wavelengths removed by allowed lower-to-higher atomic transitions.
Require photon energy hν = hc/λ to match the atomic energy gap.
Use sodium absorption near 589 nm as an example and contrast upward absorption with downward emission.
State that lower-state population, transition rules, environment, broadening, and instrumentation govern whether and how a line is observed.

accepted_variants: An orbital is a quantum state or wavefunction whose squared magnitude gives an electron probability distribution.
An atomic orbital is labeled by n, l, and ml and can contain no more than two opposite-spin electrons.
Orbitals are probability distributions, not miniature planetary orbits.
cards.definition: An atomic **orbital** is a one-electron wavefunction ψ, labeled in an atom by quantum numbers n, l, and ml; |ψ|² gives a probability-density distribution for finding the electron. The 2p subshell has n = 2 and l = 1, with ml = −1, 0, or +1; a particular 2p orbital is one member of that three-orbital set. Any single spatial orbital can hold at most two electrons with opposite spins. Orbitals organize electron configurations and help explain bonding and spectra, but they are not circular trajectories or hard-edged containers. Hydrogenic orbitals are exact one-electron solutions for hydrogen-like atoms; in many-electron atoms, orbital pictures are useful approximations within an electron-interaction model.
major_error_concepts: Defining an orbital as a fixed circular path followed by an electron.
Claiming a single spatial orbital can hold more than two electrons.
Treating an orbital boundary drawing as a surface outside which electron probability is exactly zero.
cards.prompt: Define an atomic orbital in the quantum model, state how quantum numbers and |ψ|² describe it, give a 2p orbital as an example, state its electron capacity, contrast it with a classical orbit, and state the one-electron versus many-electron model boundary.
required_concepts: Define an orbital as a one-electron wavefunction and interpret |ψ|² as probability density rather than a trajectory.
Identify n, l, and ml as orbital labels and give a 2p orbital as an example.
State that one spatial orbital can hold at most two electrons with opposite spins.
Contrast orbitals with classical fixed paths and state that many-electron orbitals are model-dependent approximations.

accepted_variants: A shell groups all atomic orbitals with the same n value.
The third shell has s, p, and d subshells, nine orbitals total, and an eighteen-electron maximum.
A shell is a quantum-number grouping rather than a sharply bounded physical layer.
cards.definition: An electron **shell** is the collection of atomic orbitals sharing the same principal quantum number n. Shell n contains n subshells, n² spatial orbitals, and can hold at most 2n² electrons. Thus n = 3 contains 3s, 3p, and 3d subshells with 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 orbitals and capacity 18 electrons. A shell is broader than a subshell, and each subshell contains individual orbitals; it is not a hard spherical layer. In a hydrogen-like atom, states with the same n are degenerate in the simplest model, whereas electron interactions in many-electron atoms make energy depend on both n and subshell.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the n = 3 shell has only three orbitals rather than three subshells and nine orbitals.
Using n² as the maximum electron count instead of the number of spatial orbitals.
Treating every orbital with the same n as exactly equal in energy in all many-electron atoms.
cards.prompt: Define an electron shell by principal quantum number n. For n = 3, list its subshells, calculate the number of orbitals and maximum electrons, contrast a shell with a subshell and orbital, and state the energy-ordering boundary for many-electron atoms.
required_concepts: Define a shell as all orbitals with the same principal quantum number n.
State that shell n contains n subshells, n² orbitals, and at most 2n² electrons.
For n = 3, identify 3s, 3p, and 3d and calculate 9 orbitals with capacity 18 electrons.
Contrast shell, subshell, and orbital and state that many-electron energy ordering is not determined by n alone.

accepted_variants: A subshell groups orbitals with common principal and angular-momentum quantum numbers.
A d subshell has five orbitals and can contain ten electrons.
The allowed l values in shell n run from zero through n minus one.
cards.definition: A **subshell** is the set of orbitals within shell n that share angular-momentum quantum number l. The labels s, p, d, and f correspond to l = 0, 1, 2, and 3. A subshell has ml values from −l through +l, giving 2l + 1 orbitals and capacity 2(2l + 1) electrons. The 3d subshell has n = 3 and l = 2, so it contains five orbitals and at most ten electrons. A shell contains one or more subshells, and a subshell contains individual orbitals. Only l = 0, 1, ..., n − 1 is allowed, so a 2d subshell does not exist.
major_error_concepts: Calling 3d a single orbital instead of a five-orbital subshell.
Claiming a d subshell can hold five rather than ten electrons.
Allowing a 2d subshell even though l = 2 is not less than n = 2.
cards.prompt: Define a subshell by n and l, relate s, p, d, and f to l, calculate the orbital and electron capacities of 3d, contrast a subshell with a shell and an orbital, and state the allowed-l boundary.
required_concepts: Define a subshell as orbitals sharing n and l within a shell.
Map s, p, d, and f to l = 0, 1, 2, and 3 and state ml = −l through +l.
Use 2l + 1 and 2(2l + 1) to calculate five orbitals and ten electrons for 3d.
Contrast shell, subshell, and orbital and enforce l < n, including that 2d is forbidden.

accepted_variants: Neutral ground-state oxygen is 1s2 2s2 2p4, with the three 2p orbitals occupied as one pair and two parallel unpaired electrons.
Electron configurations distribute a specified species' electrons subject to orbital energy, Pauli exclusion, and Hund's rule.
A correct configuration preserves the total electron count; the basic filling mnemonic needs adjustment for known exceptions, ions, and excited states.
cards.definition: An **electron configuration** assigns a specified atom or ion's electrons to orbitals. First determine electron count from atomic number and charge and specify ground or excited state; then fill available orbitals in the applicable energy order, allowing at most two opposite-spin electrons per orbital by Pauli exclusion and placing electrons singly with parallel spins across degenerate orbitals before pairing by Hund's rule. Neutral oxygen has 8 electrons, so its ground-state configuration is 1s2 2s2 2p4, with 2p occupancy [↑↓][↑][↑]. The superscripts sum to 8, preserving the electron-count invariant, and the outer occupancy helps predict oxygen's valence behavior. The simple Aufbau order is a ground-state model with known transition-metal exceptions such as Cr and Cu and does not describe every ion, excited state, or exact orbital energy without adjustment.
major_error_concepts: Pairing both 2p electrons in one orbital before singly occupying the other degenerate 2p orbitals.
Writing an oxygen configuration whose superscripts do not sum to eight electrons.
Treating the simple Aufbau sequence as exception-free or using a neutral-atom configuration without adjusting for ionic charge.
cards.prompt: Construct the ground-state electron configuration of neutral oxygen (Z = 8). State the species and state preconditions, apply energy ordering, Pauli exclusion, and Hund's rule in order, show the 2p occupancy, verify the electron-count invariant, explain one chemical use, and give a failure mode of blindly applying the simplest filling order.
required_concepts: Specify species, charge, electron count, and ground-versus-excited-state preconditions before constructing a configuration.
Apply energy ordering, Pauli exclusion, and Hund's rule as distinct ordered constraints.
Construct oxygen as 1s2 2s2 2p4 with 2p occupancy [↑↓][↑][↑] and verify that the superscripts total 8.
Connect outer occupancy to chemical use and identify blind simple-Aufbau application to transition-metal exceptions, ions, or excited states as a failure mode.

accepted_variants: Valence electrons are the outer or chemically active electrons most involved in bonding.
Sulfur has six valence electrons from 3s2 3p4.
For main-group elements the highest-n electrons are valence, but transition-metal d electrons may also participate.
cards.definition: A **valence electron** occupies an atom's outer or otherwise chemically active orbitals and participates most directly in bonding and ion formation. For a main-group atom, valence electrons are normally those in the highest principal shell. Sulfur has [Ne] 3s2 3p4, so its n = 3 shell contains six valence electrons; the [Ne] electrons are core electrons. This outer pattern helps explain sulfur's group placement and bonding possibilities. For transition metals, chemically active (n − 1)d electrons can also be valence electrons, so counting only the highest-n shell is an incomplete universal rule.
major_error_concepts: Counting all sixteen electrons in sulfur as valence electrons.
Counting only the two 3s electrons and ignoring sulfur's four 3p valence electrons.
Applying the highest-n-only rule to every transition metal without qualification.
cards.prompt: Define a valence electron, use neutral sulfur's [Ne] 3s2 3p4 configuration to identify and count its valence electrons, contrast valence with core electrons, connect the count to bonding, and state the transition-metal boundary.
required_concepts: Define valence electrons by outer or chemically active orbitals and contrast them with core electrons.
Read [Ne] 3s2 3p4 and count six main-group valence electrons for sulfur.
Connect valence occupancy to bonding, ion formation, and periodic-group behavior.
State that transition-metal d electrons make the highest-principal-shell shortcut incomplete.

accepted_variants: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge or attraction an electron feels after electron shielding.
The introductory estimate is nuclear charge minus an effective shielding constant.
A simple sodium-core estimate gives the 3s electron an effective charge near plus one, but this is not sodium's exact ionic charge.
cards.definition: **Effective nuclear charge**, Zeff, describes the net positive nuclear attraction experienced by a particular electron after screening by other electrons. A qualitative model writes Zeff ≈ Z − S, where Z is nuclear charge and S is an effective shielding constant. Treating sodium's ten core electrons as roughly screening its 3s electron gives Z = 11, S ≈ 10, and Zeff ≈ +1 as an introductory estimate. Across a period, Z rises while shielding by electrons in the same shell rises less effectively, so valence-electron Zeff generally increases. Zeff is electron- and orbital-dependent; S is not simply an exact universal count, and Zeff is neither the atom's formal ionic charge nor a literal reduction of proton number.
major_error_concepts: Defining Zeff as the actual number of protons remaining after electrons cancel nuclear charge.
Treating S as exactly the number of all other electrons for every orbital and atom.
Equating effective nuclear charge with the formal charge of an atom or ion.
cards.prompt: Define effective nuclear charge and the qualitative estimate Zeff ≈ Z − S. Use a simple core-screening model for sodium's 3s electron with Z = 11 and S ≈ 10, explain the across-period trend, and state why the estimate is not an exact ionic charge or universal calculation.
required_concepts: Define Zeff as the net nuclear attraction experienced by a specified electron after shielding.
State the qualitative relation Zeff ≈ Z − S and identify Z and S.
Use Z = 11 and a simple S ≈ 10 core-screening estimate to obtain Zeff ≈ +1 for sodium's 3s electron.
Explain the general across-period increase and state that Zeff is orbital-dependent, approximate, and distinct from ionic charge.

accepted_variants: Shielding is the partial reduction of nuclear attraction experienced by an electron because other electrons screen the nucleus.
Lithium's two 1s core electrons substantially shield its outer 2s electron.
More penetrating orbitals feel less shielding and greater effective nuclear attraction.
cards.definition: **Shielding** is the reduction in nuclear attraction felt by an electron because electron-electron repulsion and intervening electron density partially screen the nucleus. In lithium, the 1s2 core lies mostly inside the 2s valence distribution and substantially shields the 2s electron from Z = 3. Inner-shell electrons generally shield outer electrons more effectively than electrons in the same shell, and greater orbital penetration exposes an electron to more nuclear attraction; for a given shell, s orbitals penetrate more than p, d, or f. Shielding does not change the proton count or fully neutralize the nucleus, and it is not identical for every electron or orbital.
major_error_concepts: Claiming that shielding removes protons from the nucleus or changes atomic number.
Assuming each other electron contributes identical complete screening.
Claiming same-shell electrons shield as completely as compact inner-shell electrons or ignoring orbital penetration.
cards.prompt: Define electron shielding, use lithium's 1s2 core and 2s valence electron as a structural example, explain why inner-shell shielding is stronger than same-shell shielding and how penetration matters, contrast shielding with changing nuclear charge, and state its incomplete-screening boundary.
required_concepts: Define shielding as partial screening of nuclear attraction by other electrons and electron-electron repulsion.
Use lithium's inner 1s2 electrons shielding its outer 2s electron as a particle-level example.
Explain that inner-shell shielding is generally stronger than same-shell shielding and that orbital penetration changes exposure to the nucleus.
State that shielding is incomplete, orbital-dependent, and does not alter nuclear charge.

accepted_variants: A periodic group is a vertical column of elements, whereas a period is a horizontal row.
Main-group elements in the same column often share a valence configuration pattern and related chemical behavior.
Group 1 includes lithium and sodium with ns1; group 17 includes fluorine and chlorine with ns2np5.
cards.definition: A periodic-table **group** is a vertical column, numbered 1 through 18. Main-group elements in a group usually share a characteristic valence-electron pattern that helps explain related chemistry: group 1 includes Li and Na with an ns1 pattern, while group 17 includes F and Cl with an ns2np5 pattern. A group is vertical; a period is a horizontal row associated with filling a new principal shell. Similarity is a trend, not identity: helium has 1s2 yet is placed in group 18 because of its closed shell and noble-gas behavior, and transition-metal group patterns are less reducible to a single outer-shell electron count.
major_error_concepts: Calling a horizontal row a group and a vertical column a period.
Claiming that every member of a group has identical reactivity or an identical full electron configuration.
Ignoring helium's 1s2 exception or treating transition-metal group behavior as a simple main-group electron-count rule.
cards.prompt: Define a periodic-table group, identify representative members and valence patterns for groups 1 and 17, explain why main-group members often have related chemistry, contrast a group with a period, and state both the helium-placement and transition-metal boundaries.
required_concepts: Define a group as a vertical column numbered 1 through 18.
Identify Li and Na in group 1 with ns1 and F and Cl in group 17 with ns2np5.
Explain that related main-group chemistry arises in part from shared valence-electron patterns and contrast vertical groups with horizontal periods.
State helium's closed-shell placement in group 18 and the less regular valence patterns of transition metals as boundary cases.

accepted_variants: A period is a horizontal row in which atomic number rises, a new principal shell begins, and the row's energetically available subshells progressively fill.
Period 2 runs from lithium to neon, filling 2s and then 2p while main-group valence behavior changes across the row.
The f-block rows displayed below the table are continuations of periods 6 and 7, not separate periods.
cards.definition: A periodic-table **period** is a horizontal row. Atomic number increases by one from each element to the next. A period begins when a new principal shell becomes occupied, and the energetically available subshells associated with the row then fill; longer periods include interleaved (n − 1)d or (n − 2)f filling rather than only subshells with the period's principal quantum number. Across period 2, Li and Be fill 2s, then B through Ne fill 2p; main-group valence count generally progresses from one for Li to eight for Ne, producing systematic changes in chemistry. A period is horizontal, whereas a group is vertical and usually shares a valence pattern. Period 1 contains only H and He because n = 1 has only 1s, and the lanthanides and actinides belong within periods 6 and 7 even though they are conventionally displayed below the main table.
major_error_concepts: Calling a vertical column a period and a horizontal row a group.
Claiming every element in one period has the same valence-electron pattern or similar chemistry.
Treating the detached lanthanide and actinide display as periods 8 and 9.
cards.prompt: Define a periodic-table period, trace representative elements across period 2 from Li through Ne, connect the progression to atomic number, principal-shell and subshell occupation, and valence behavior, contrast a period with a group, and state the period-1 and separated-f-block boundaries.
required_concepts: Define a period as a horizontal row and contrast it with a vertical group.
Trace period 2 from Li through Ne as atomic number increases one unit at a time and 2s then 2p orbitals fill.
Relate the left-to-right occupation pattern to changing main-group valence counts and chemical behavior.
State that period 1 has only H and He and that the separately drawn lanthanides and actinides remain parts of periods 6 and 7.

accepted_variants: Metals generally have delocalized valence electrons and are conductive, lustrous, malleable, or ductile in bulk.
Copper is a metal whose mobile electronic states account for strong electrical conductivity and whose nondirectional bonding permits deformation.
Metallic properties are trends that vary with element, crystal structure, phase, temperature, and purity.
cards.definition: **Metals** are elements whose condensed phases usually contain relatively mobile, delocalized valence electrons around positive atomic cores. In copper metal, this extended electronic structure supports electrical and thermal conductivity, metallic luster, and the ability of atomic layers to shift without breaking a set of localized directional bonds, producing malleability and ductility. Metals also often form cations. These are trends, not a single defining checklist: mercury is liquid near room temperature, some metals are brittle or poor conductors relative to copper, and reactivity varies widely. Metallic character also depends on phase, structure, temperature, purity, and pressure.
major_error_concepts: Defining a metal solely as any solid that conducts electricity.
Claiming all metals are solid, highly conductive, unreactive, or malleable under every condition.
Treating delocalized electrons as electrons that have left the material entirely rather than remaining part of its electronic structure.
cards.prompt: Define metals at particle and bulk scales, use copper as a structural example, connect delocalized valence electrons with conductivity and malleability, contrast metals with nonmetals, and give exceptions showing why metallic properties are trends rather than an absolute checklist.
required_concepts: Describe metals through delocalized valence electrons and positive atomic cores at particle scale.
Connect copper's extended electronic structure to bulk conductivity, luster, malleability, and ductility.
Contrast typical metallic behavior with localized-electron nonmetal behavior and mention common cation formation.
State exceptions such as liquid mercury and brittle or comparatively resistive metals and limit claims to specified conditions and phases.

accepted_variants: Nonmetals generally lack metallic delocalized-electron conduction and tend to gain or share valence electrons.
Oxygen is a molecular gaseous nonmetal, while solid sulfur is brittle and poorly conducting.
Nonmetal is a periodic and electronic category, not a guarantee that every sample is an electrical insulator.
cards.definition: **Nonmetals** are elements that generally lack the extended delocalized-electron structure characteristic of metals. Their valence electrons are often localized in atoms, molecules, or directional covalent bonds, and nonmetal atoms commonly gain electrons or share them in bonding. Oxygen exists as molecular O2 gas, while solid sulfur is brittle and a poor electrical conductor. Nonmetals span gases, a liquid, and solids, so no single macroscopic property defines all of them. Graphite, an allotrope of carbon, conducts along its layers, and chemical behavior varies with allotrope, structure, phase, temperature, and pressure.
major_error_concepts: Defining every nonmetal as a brittle solid even though many are gases and bromine is liquid near room temperature.
Claiming nonmetals can only gain electrons and never form covalent bonds by sharing electron density.
Using graphite's conductivity to classify carbon as a metal without considering its bonding structure and other properties.
cards.prompt: Define nonmetals at particle and bulk scales, use oxygen and solid sulfur as examples, connect localized or shared valence electrons with characteristic bonding and conduction, contrast nonmetals with metals, and state graphite and physical-state boundaries.
required_concepts: Describe nonmetals through relatively localized or shared valence electrons and common electron gain or covalent sharing.
Use O2 gas and brittle, poorly conducting solid sulfur as particle-to-bulk examples.
Contrast typical nonmetal behavior with metallic delocalization and common cation formation.
State that nonmetals occupy multiple physical states and that graphite and allotrope-dependent behavior prevent an absolute property checklist.

accepted_variants: Metalloids are elements with properties intermediate between those of metals and nonmetals.
A metalloid is an element whose physical and chemical behavior lies between metallic and nonmetallic behavior, often including semiconductivity.
Silicon is a brittle covalent-network semiconductor whose conductivity can be tuned, illustrating mixed metallic and nonmetallic behavior.
cards.definition: **Metalloids** are elements whose properties are intermediate between those of metals and nonmetals. Many are brittle solids and semiconductors, and they commonly occur near the staircase boundary of the periodic table; the classification is based on behavior rather than a single exact property. Silicon provides a structural example: its covalent network gives a controllable electronic band gap, so temperature and doping can strongly change conductivity while the bulk crystal remains brittle rather than malleable. Common lists include B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, and Te, but sources differ near the staircase, and neither membership nor behavior is fixed by position alone.
major_error_concepts: Treating metalloids as a compound class rather than as individual elements.
Assuming every element adjacent to the staircase is unambiguously a metalloid or that all metalloids have identical properties.
Defining a metalloid solely by periodic-table position without considering structure and measured behavior.
cards.prompt: Define metalloids, locate their conventional periodic-table region, use silicon as a particle-to-bulk semiconductor example, contrast them with metals and nonmetals, and explain why the membership boundary and properties are not absolute.
required_concepts: Identify metalloids as elements intermediate in properties between metals and nonmetals.
Relate the category to the periodic-table staircase region and characteristic semiconducting or mixed behavior without treating the boundary as absolute.
Use silicon's covalent network, band gap, tunable conductivity, and brittleness as a particle-to-bulk example.
Contrast metalloids with metals and nonmetals and state that accepted membership lists and properties vary by source, structure, temperature, and doping.

accepted_variants: Atomic radius is a convention-based size such as half the distance between identical bonded nuclei.
A 198.8 pm Cl–Cl distance gives a 99.4 pm covalent chlorine radius.
Atomic size usually decreases across a period and increases down a group, but quoted values depend on the chosen structural definition.
cards.definition: An atom has no sharp classical edge, so **atomic radius** is convention-dependent. A covalent radius is commonly half the internuclear distance in a homonuclear bond; metallic and van der Waals radii use different structural contacts. For d(Cl–Cl) = 198.8 ± 0.4 pm, division by the exact count 2 gives r = 99.4 ± 0.2 pm = (9.94 ± 0.02) × 10^-11 m. Within a consistent convention, radius generally decreases across a period as effective nuclear charge increases and increases down a group as occupied shells are added. Values depend on bonding, coordination, oxidation state, and measurement model, so numerical comparisons require the same radius definition.
major_error_concepts: Treating an atom as a hard sphere with one exact context-independent radius.
Reporting 198.8 pm rather than half that distance as the covalent radius of one chlorine atom.
Comparing a van der Waals radius directly with a covalent radius as though the definitions were interchangeable.
cards.prompt: Define atomic radius operationally. A Cl–Cl internuclear distance is 198.8 ± 0.4 pm; calculate the covalent radius and convert it to meters with appropriate uncertainty and significant figures. State the periodic trend and why radii from different conventions should not be mixed.
required_concepts: Define atomic radius operationally and distinguish covalent, metallic, and van der Waals conventions from a sharp atomic boundary.
Calculate half of 198.8 ± 0.4 pm as 99.4 ± 0.2 pm and convert it to (9.94 ± 0.02) × 10^-11 m.
Report units, uncertainty, and significant figures consistently, recognizing that division by the count 2 is exact.
Explain the general across-period decrease and down-group increase using effective nuclear charge and added occupied shells, while limiting comparisons to one convention.

accepted_variants: Ionic radius is an effective crystal-derived ion size whose value depends on coordination and convention.
Under the stated NaCl partition, sodium ion radius is 102 pm or 1.02 × 10^-10 m.
Cations are commonly smaller and anions larger than their parent atoms, but ionic radii are environment-dependent.
cards.definition: An **ionic radius** is an effective ion size inferred by partitioning measured interionic distances in a crystal under a stated coordination and radius convention. If d(Na+–Cl−) = 283 pm and the convention assigns r(Cl−) = 181 pm, then r(Na+) = 283 − 181 = 102 pm = 1.02 × 10^-10 m. Cations are usually smaller than their neutral parent atoms because electron loss reduces repulsion and may remove an occupied shell; anions are usually larger because added electron density increases repulsion. Within an isoelectronic series, greater nuclear charge generally gives smaller radius. Ionic radius is not directly unique: oxidation state, coordination number, spin state, structure, and tabulation convention change the value.
major_error_concepts: Treating ionic radius as one exact isolated-ion boundary independent of crystal environment.
Adding 283 and 181 pm instead of subtracting the assigned chloride contribution.
Claiming every ion is smaller than its neutral atom, including anions formed by electron gain.
cards.prompt: Define ionic radius operationally. In one six-coordinate NaCl radius convention, the Na+–Cl− distance is 283 pm and r(Cl−) is assigned 181 pm; calculate r(Na+) in pm and meters. Compare ions with neutral parents and state the coordination and convention boundary.
required_concepts: Define ionic radius as a convention-dependent partition of crystal interionic distances rather than a directly observed hard boundary.
Calculate 283 pm − 181 pm = 102 pm = 1.02 × 10^-10 m for Na+ under the stated convention.
Explain why cations are usually smaller and anions larger than their neutral parent atoms and state the isoelectronic nuclear-charge trend.
Require specified ion, oxidation state, coordination, structure, and radius convention before comparing numerical values.

accepted_variants: First ionization energy is the energy needed to remove the first electron from a gaseous ground-state atom.
Sodium's 5.139 eV per atom corresponds to 495.8 kJ per mole of atoms.
Ionization energy usually rises across a period and falls down a group, with configuration-based exceptions.
cards.definition: The **first ionization energy** is the minimum energy required to remove one electron from each gaseous ground-state atom: X(g) → X+(g) + e−. It is positive because energy must be supplied. For sodium, 5.139 eV per atom × 96.485 kJ mol^-1 per eV = 495.8 kJ/mol to four significant figures. First ionization energy generally increases across a period as effective attraction rises and decreases down a group as valence electrons become farther and more shielded, with subshell and electron-pairing exceptions. Successive ionization energies remove further electrons from gaseous ions and are distinct quantities, often showing a large jump after all valence electrons are removed.
major_error_concepts: Defining ionization energy for removing an electron from a solid or solution without specifying conversion to the gas-phase atomic process.
Treating first ionization energy as energy released rather than required.
Assuming every element follows a perfectly monotonic periodic trend or that all successive ionizations have the first-ionization value.
cards.prompt: Define first ionization energy with a gas-phase equation. Convert sodium's 5.139 eV per atom to kJ/mol using 1 eV per particle = 96.485 kJ/mol, report appropriate precision, explain its periodic trend, and distinguish first from successive ionizations.
required_concepts: Define first ionization energy with X(g) → X+(g) + e− for a gaseous ground-state atom and state that energy input is positive.
Convert 5.139 eV per atom to 495.8 kJ/mol using 96.485 kJ mol^-1 per eV and retain four significant figures.
Explain the general across-period increase and down-group decrease through effective attraction, atomic size, shielding, and electron configuration.
Distinguish first ionization from successive ionizations and recognize large post-valence jumps and trend exceptions.

accepted_variants: Under the thermochemical convention, electron affinity is the enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron.
Chlorine electron addition has ΔH about −349 kJ/mol, meaning roughly 3.62 eV is released per atom.
A positive tabulated electron-affinity number may mean energy released, so its sign convention must be declared.
cards.definition: Using the thermochemical convention, the **first electron affinity** is the enthalpy change for adding an electron to a gaseous species: X(g) + e− → X−(g). For chlorine, ΔH ≈ −349 kJ/mol, so addition is exothermic and releases 349 kJ per mole of Cl atoms, a magnitude of 349/96.485 = 3.62 eV per atom to three significant figures. Some tables instead report electron affinity as a positive energy-released magnitude, so the convention and sign must always be stated. Electron affinity concerns electron addition, unlike positive ionization energy for removal. Values show periodic trends but important subshell, electron-repulsion, noble-gas, and second-electron-affinity exceptions; the second addition to an already negative ion is generally endothermic.
major_error_concepts: Quoting an electron-affinity sign without stating whether it means process enthalpy or positive energy released.
Defining electron affinity as electron removal or confusing it with ionization energy.
Assuming every first electron addition is exothermic or that adding a second electron has the same energy change.
cards.prompt: Define first electron affinity using the thermochemical ΔH convention and a gas-phase equation. Interpret chlorine's ΔH ≈ −349 kJ/mol at particle and molar scales, convert the released-energy magnitude to eV per atom, contrast electron affinity with ionization energy, and state sign-convention and exception boundaries.
required_concepts: Define the thermochemical process X(g) + e− → X−(g) and declare that its electron-affinity value is ΔH under the chosen convention.
Interpret chlorine's −349 kJ/mol as exothermic electron addition and convert the released magnitude to 3.62 eV per atom.
Contrast electron addition with ionization-energy electron removal and distinguish signed ΔH from tables reporting a positive released-energy magnitude.
State that gaseous-state, subshell, repulsion, noble-gas, and successive-electron boundaries produce important exceptions.

accepted_variants: Electronegativity is a dimensionless relative measure of a bonded atom's attraction for shared electrons.
Fluorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so HF has electron density shifted toward F and Δχ = 1.78 on the Pauling scale.
Electronegativity is scale-dependent and is not the same quantity as electron affinity or formal atomic charge.
cards.definition: **Electronegativity** is a relative, dimensionless measure of how strongly an atom in a bond attracts shared electron density. On the Pauling scale, χ(H) = 2.20 and χ(F) = 3.98, so Δχ = 1.78 and the H–F bonding density is shifted toward F, giving Hδ+–Fδ− and a polar bond. This particle-level redistribution contributes to molecular dipoles and chemical reactivity. Electronegativity is not the gas-phase energy change called electron affinity and is not a directly measured isolated-atom charge. Different scales give different numbers, noble-gas values may be undefined, and no universal Δχ cutoff sharply separates covalent from ionic bonding.
major_error_concepts: Assigning the negative end of H–F to hydrogen even though fluorine has the larger electronegativity.
Giving electronegativity units of kJ/mol or treating it as the energy change for adding an electron.
Using one Δχ threshold as an exception-free law that labels every bond purely ionic or purely covalent.
cards.prompt: Define electronegativity as a bonded-atom property, use Pauling values H = 2.20 and F = 3.98 to interpret the H–F bond, connect the particle-level electron-density shift with observable polarity, contrast electronegativity with electron affinity, and state scale and cutoff boundaries.
required_concepts: Define electronegativity as a relative attraction for shared electron density by an atom in a bond and state that the scale is dimensionless.
Calculate Δχ = 3.98 − 2.20 = 1.78 for H–F and assign Hδ+ and Fδ− from the density shift.
Connect electron-density polarization to molecular dipoles or reactivity and contrast electronegativity with gas-phase electron affinity.
State that values depend on scale, may be unavailable for noble gases, and do not provide a universal sharp ionic-covalent cutoff.

accepted_variants: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction among oppositely charged ions in an extended structure.
NaCl crystal contains a repeating Na+ and Cl− lattice represented by formula units rather than individual NaCl molecules.
Ionic solids are often high-melting and brittle; they conduct when ions become mobile in a melt or solution.
cards.definition: An **ionic bond** is the electrostatic attraction among oppositely charged ions, normally acting throughout an extended ionic structure rather than as an isolated two-particle link. Crystalline NaCl contains alternating Na+ and Cl− environments in a lattice; NaCl is a 1:1 formula-unit ratio, not a collection of discrete NaCl molecules. Strong attractions contribute to high melting temperature, while shifting a lattice plane can align like charges and cause brittle fracture. Solid ions are not mobile enough for ordinary electrical conduction, but molten or dissolved ions can carry current. Ionic and covalent descriptions form a continuum: polarization can give nominally ionic compounds appreciable covalent character.
major_error_concepts: Describing an NaCl crystal as isolated covalent Na–Cl molecules.
Claiming an ionic solid conducts well merely because it contains charged particles, without requiring mobile ions.
Treating electron transfer and ionic versus covalent character as an all-or-nothing boundary with no polarization.
cards.prompt: Define ionic bonding at particle and bulk scales using crystalline NaCl. Explain cation-anion attraction, formula-unit versus molecule language, characteristic bulk properties and conduction states, contrast ionic with localized covalent bonding, and state the partial-covalency boundary.
required_concepts: Define ionic bonding as extended electrostatic attraction between cations and anions.
Use crystalline NaCl to distinguish a 1:1 formula unit in a lattice from a discrete molecule.
Connect lattice-scale attraction to high melting behavior and brittleness and distinguish solid from molten or dissolved conduction.
Contrast ionic with covalent bonding while stating that real compounds can have mixed or polarized character.

accepted_variants: A covalent bond is stabilizing shared electron density between atomic nuclei.
The H–H bond contains a shared pair concentrated between two hydrogen nuclei.
Covalent bonding includes molecular and network structures and may be nonpolar or polar.
cards.definition: A **covalent bond** arises when shared electron density between nuclei lowers the system's energy relative to separated atoms. In H2, two H atoms contribute electrons to a bonding state concentrated between the nuclei; a Lewis model represents this as one shared pair, H–H. Covalent bonds can form discrete molecules or extended networks such as diamond, whose macroscopic hardness does not imply discrete C molecules. Sharing need not be equal, so covalent bonds can be polar. Covalent, ionic, and metallic models emphasize different electron distributions and are not perfectly sharp categories; bond strength and properties depend on atoms, geometry, environment, and electronic state.
major_error_concepts: Defining a covalent bond as two electrons orbiting on a fixed line between atoms.
Assuming every covalently bonded substance consists of discrete molecules, excluding network solids.
Claiming covalent bonds always share electrons equally or that ionic and covalent character cannot mix.
cards.prompt: Define a covalent bond at electron-density and macroscopic-structure scales, use H2 as an example, contrast localized covalent, ionic, and metallic descriptions, and state polar-bond and network-solid boundaries.
required_concepts: Define covalent bonding through shared electron density between nuclei and connect sharing with energetic stabilization.
Use H2 and its shared electron pair as a particle-level and structural example.
Distinguish discrete covalent molecules from extended covalent networks and contrast localized sharing with ionic and metallic descriptions.
State that sharing can be unequal and that bond categories and properties depend on chemical environment.

accepted_variants: Metallic bonding joins positive atomic cores through valence electrons delocalized across a solid.
Copper's extended electronic states support conduction, while nondirectional cohesion permits deformation.
The electron-sea picture is qualitative; real metallic properties require band and crystal structure.
cards.definition: **Metallic bonding** is cohesion among positive atomic cores and valence electrons delocalized across many sites in a metal. In crystalline copper, overlapping orbitals form extended electronic states, allowing charge and thermal energy to move through the lattice and allowing layers to shift without breaking a fixed set of directional bonds; these mechanisms support conductivity and malleability. Unlike ionic bonding, cohesion is not attraction between separate cation and anion sublattices, and unlike a localized covalent bond, the electrons are not assigned to one atom pair. The simple electron-sea picture is qualitative; band structure, crystal defects, alloying, temperature, and phase determine actual behavior.
major_error_concepts: Describing a metal as a lattice of fully isolated cations surrounded by electrons that have left the material.
Treating metallic bonding as a collection of fixed two-atom covalent bonds.
Claiming every metal has identical conductivity or malleability independent of phase, temperature, defects, and composition.
cards.prompt: Define metallic bonding at particle and bulk scales using crystalline copper, relate delocalized electronic states to conductivity and nondirectional cohesion, contrast metallic with ionic and localized covalent bonding, and state the band-model and material-condition boundaries.
required_concepts: Define metallic bonding as cohesion between positive atomic cores and valence electrons delocalized over many lattice sites.
Use crystalline copper to connect extended electronic states with conductivity and nondirectional cohesion with malleability.
Contrast metallic bonding with oppositely charged ionic sublattices and localized pairwise covalent bonding.
State that the electron-sea description is a model and that bands, defects, alloying, temperature, and phase control measured properties.

accepted_variants: A cation is a positively charged ion with fewer electrons than total protons.
Sodium forms Na+ by losing one electron while its eleven-proton nucleus remains unchanged.
Positive polyatomic ions can also form by protonation, so cation formation is not universally simple electron loss.
cards.definition: A **cation** is an ion with net positive charge because its total proton count exceeds its electron count. A neutral Na atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons; Na → Na+ + e− leaves the nucleus unchanged but gives Na+ 11 protons and 10 electrons, so its charge is +1. Cations combine with anions in charge-balanced ionic matter and move toward the cathode during electrolysis. Monatomic cations commonly form by electron loss, but protonation can make a polyatomic cation without net electron loss from the original molecule, as NH3 + H+ → NH4+. Positive charge does not mean the species contains only positive particles.
major_error_concepts: Claiming Na+ has gained a proton or lost a proton from its nucleus during ordinary ion formation.
Defining positive charge as having no electrons rather than having fewer electrons than protons.
Claiming every cation must form by electron loss and excluding protonated polyatomic ions.
cards.prompt: Define a cation using proton and electron counts, show how Na forms Na+, connect positive ions to macroscopic ionic matter, contrast cations with anions, and state the electron-loss versus protonation boundary.
required_concepts: Define a cation by proton count exceeding electron count and distinguish net charge from the signs of all constituent particles.
Use Na → Na+ + e− to preserve 11 protons while changing from 11 to 10 electrons and obtaining +1 charge.
Connect cations with charge-balanced ionic matter and contrast them with negatively charged anions.
State that electron loss is common for monatomic cations but protonation can form polyatomic cations such as NH4+.

accepted_variants: An anion is a negatively charged ion with more electrons than total protons.
Chlorine forms Cl− by gaining one electron while its seventeen-proton nucleus remains unchanged.
Negative polyatomic ions can form by deprotonation, so anion formation is not universally simple electron gain.
cards.definition: An **anion** is an ion with net negative charge because its electron count exceeds its total proton count. A neutral Cl atom has 17 protons and 17 electrons; Cl + e− → Cl− leaves the nucleus unchanged but gives Cl− 18 electrons, so its charge is −1. Anions combine with cations in charge-balanced ionic matter and move toward the anode during electrolysis. Monatomic anions commonly form by electron gain, but deprotonation can form a polyatomic anion without adding an electron to the original molecule, as H2O → H+ + OH−. Negative charge does not mean the species contains no protons.
major_error_concepts: Claiming Cl− forms by removing a proton from chlorine's nucleus.
Defining negative charge as absence of protons rather than an excess of electrons over protons.
Claiming every anion must form by electron gain and excluding deprotonated polyatomic ions.
cards.prompt: Define an anion using proton and electron counts, show how Cl forms Cl−, connect negative ions to macroscopic ionic matter, contrast anions with cations, and state the electron-gain versus deprotonation boundary.
required_concepts: Define an anion by electron count exceeding total proton count and distinguish net charge from the presence of protons.
Use Cl + e− → Cl− to preserve 17 protons while changing from 17 to 18 electrons and obtaining −1 charge.
Connect anions with charge-balanced ionic matter and contrast them with positively charged cations.
State that electron gain is common for monatomic anions but deprotonation can form polyatomic anions such as OH−.

accepted_variants: A crystal lattice is an ideal periodic array of equivalent repeating sites.
A crystal structure combines a lattice with a basis of atoms, ions, or molecules.
NaCl has an extended repeating ionic crystal rather than separate NaCl molecules.
cards.definition: A crystal **lattice** is an ideal periodic array of points representing equivalent repeating environments. A physical crystal is described by attaching a basis of atoms, ions, or molecules to those points; the points themselves are not necessarily literal particles. In NaCl, a repeating ionic arrangement generates an extended crystal whose formula gives a ratio rather than one discrete molecule. Microscopic translational repetition accounts for long-range order and diffraction in the bulk. Real crystals are finite, contain surfaces, defects, thermal motion, and sometimes disorder, while amorphous materials lack the same long-range periodic lattice even when they have local structure.
major_error_concepts: Equating every abstract lattice point with one particular atom without specifying a basis.
Treating a lattice as a single molecule or one formula unit.
Claiming a real finite crystal has perfect infinite repetition with no surfaces, defects, motion, or disorder.
cards.prompt: Define a crystal lattice and distinguish it from the particles or basis associated with lattice points. Use NaCl as an ionic example, connect microscopic repetition with a macroscopic crystal, contrast a lattice with a molecule, and state defect, surface, and amorphous-material boundaries.
required_concepts: Define a lattice as a periodic array of equivalent points and distinguish the abstract lattice from its attached particle basis.
Use NaCl as an extended ionic arrangement represented by a repeating ratio rather than one discrete molecule.
Connect microscopic translational order with macroscopic crystalline structure or diffraction.
State that real crystals have finite surfaces, defects, thermal motion, and disorder and contrast them with amorphous materials.

accepted_variants: A Lewis dot symbol shows an element symbol surrounded by its valence-electron dots.
Oxygen has six valence electrons and therefore six dots in its Lewis symbol.
Lewis symbols are valence-counting diagrams, not orbital diagrams or three-dimensional electron maps.
cards.definition: A **Lewis symbol** places an element symbol inside dots representing its valence electrons. Oxygen has configuration [He] 2s2 2p4 and therefore six valence electrons; its Lewis symbol places six dots around O, conventionally placing one dot on each of four sides before pairing two sides. The symbol supports valence-electron counting and predicts available bonding or lone-pair patterns at an introductory level. It does not show core electrons, orbital energies, three-dimensional geometry, or actual electron trajectories. Main-group valence counts map cleanly to these symbols, while transition-metal valence assignments and bonding often require more detailed models.
major_error_concepts: Drawing all eight oxygen electrons as Lewis dots instead of only its six valence electrons.
Pairing dots on one side before placing one on each available side under the conventional construction rule.
Treating Lewis-dot positions as literal orbital shapes or electron trajectories.
cards.prompt: Define a Lewis symbol, construct oxygen's symbol from its six valence electrons, explain the single-before-pair dot convention and its bonding use, contrast it with a full electron configuration, and state main-group and transition-metal boundaries.
required_concepts: Define a Lewis symbol as an element symbol plus dots for valence electrons.
Use oxygen's [He] 2s2 2p4 configuration to place six dots, singly on four sides before pairing.
Connect the symbol with introductory bonding and lone-pair counting and contrast it with a full electron configuration.
State that it omits core electrons, orbital and geometric detail and is less straightforward for transition metals.

accepted_variants: A Lewis structure represents shared bonding pairs and nonbonding valence-electron pairs.
Water uses eight valence electrons: two O–H bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen.
Lewis structures are electron-counting diagrams and do not by themselves specify exact three-dimensional shape or electron density.
cards.definition: A **Lewis structure** is an electron-counting model that shows covalent bonds as shared electron pairs and nonbonding valence electrons as lone pairs for a molecule or polyatomic ion. H2O has 6 + 1 + 1 = 8 valence electrons: two O–H single bonds use four electrons, and two lone pairs on O use the remaining four. Unlike a Lewis symbol for one isolated element, a Lewis structure connects atoms and allocates the whole species' valence electrons. It can support bonding, charge, and geometry reasoning, but the drawing is not a measured three-dimensional shape, does not show orbital energies, and may require resonance or more advanced electronic models for delocalization and unusual bonding.
major_error_concepts: Counting only six total valence electrons for H2O and ignoring the hydrogen contributions.
Using all eight electrons in four O–H bonds and leaving no oxygen lone pairs.
Treating a two-dimensional Lewis drawing as a literal measured molecular geometry.
cards.prompt: Define a Lewis structure and construct H2O by counting eight valence electrons, showing two O–H bonds and two oxygen lone pairs. Explain what the diagram predicts, contrast it with a Lewis symbol and a three-dimensional structure, and state resonance and model limitations.
required_concepts: Define a Lewis structure as a valence-electron accounting model for bonds and lone pairs in a molecule or polyatomic ion.
Count eight valence electrons for H2O and allocate four to two O–H bonds and four to two oxygen lone pairs.
Contrast a multi-atom Lewis structure with a single-element Lewis symbol and with actual three-dimensional geometry.
State that resonance, delocalization, orbital energy, and unusual bonding can exceed a single Lewis diagram's regime.

accepted_variants: The octet rule says many main-group atoms tend toward eight electrons in their Lewis valence shell.
In CO2, two C=O double bonds give carbon and each oxygen an octet when lone pairs are counted.
The octet rule is a useful heuristic with electron-deficient, odd-electron, expanded-valence, and transition-metal exceptions.
cards.definition: The **octet rule** is an introductory main-group heuristic: atoms often form bonds and lone pairs that place eight electrons around a valence-shell Lewis count, analogous to a filled s and p valence shell. In O=C=O, each oxygen has two lone pairs plus a double bond, and carbon has two double bonds, so each atom is assigned an octet. The rule helps construct common main-group Lewis structures but is not a universal stability law. H follows a duet instead; BF3 is electron-deficient, NO has an odd electron, and species such as SF6 have expanded valence counts. Transition-metal bonding and many delocalized or hypervalent systems require broader models.
major_error_concepts: Treating the octet rule as exception-free or as proof that every drawn octet is a stable molecule.
Applying an octet requirement to hydrogen instead of a two-electron first shell.
Rejecting BF3, NO, or SF6 solely because it does not fit an ordinary octet pattern.
cards.prompt: Define the octet rule as a main-group Lewis heuristic, verify octets in CO2, explain its particle-level meaning and chemical use, contrast it with the duet rule, and identify electron-deficient, odd-electron, and expanded-valence exceptions.
required_concepts: Define the octet rule as a main-group Lewis-electron heuristic favoring eight valence-shell electrons, not a universal law.
Verify that carbon and both oxygens have octets in O=C=O by counting bonds and lone pairs.
Explain its use in constructing common Lewis structures and contrast it with hydrogen's duet behavior.
Identify BF3, NO, SF6, transition metals, and delocalized bonding as distinct exception or model-boundary classes.

accepted_variants: The duet rule reflects the two-electron capacity of the single 1s orbital.
Each H in H2 is assigned a shared two-electron duet, while helium already has 1s2.
Duet behavior is limited to first-shell or helium-like configurations and is not the octet rule.
cards.definition: The **duet rule** is the first-shell counterpart to the octet heuristic: the n = 1 shell contains only one 1s orbital and therefore holds at most two opposite-spin electrons. In H2, the shared pair gives each H access to two electrons in the Lewis count; He already has a filled 1s2 shell. The rule also describes helium-like configurations such as Li+, but it does not mean every species seeks exactly two total electrons. It applies to first-shell valence behavior, especially H and He-like ions, while atoms with n ≥ 2 valence shells require octet or more general electronic reasoning.
major_error_concepts: Claiming hydrogen requires eight valence electrons in an ordinary Lewis structure.
Claiming every atom or ion becomes stable only when it has exactly two total electrons.
Treating a duet as two orbitals or as permission for four electrons in the 1s shell.
cards.prompt: Define the duet rule from the capacity of the n = 1 shell, apply it to H2 and He, contrast it with the octet rule, and state which first-shell species and ionic configurations it can and cannot describe.
required_concepts: Define the duet rule through the one-orbital, two-electron capacity of the n = 1 shell.
Apply it to the shared pair in H2 and the filled 1s2 configuration of He.
Contrast first-shell duet behavior with the main-group octet heuristic for later shells.
State that helium-like ions such as Li+ can have a duet but that the rule is not a universal two-total-electron target.

accepted_variants: A polar bond has electron density shifted toward the more electronegative atom.
H–Cl is polarized Hδ+–Clδ−, whereas H–H is nonpolar by symmetry.
Bond polarity does not by itself determine whether the whole molecule has a net dipole.
cards.definition: **Bond polarity** is unequal sharing of bonding electron density caused by differences in the bonded atoms and their environments, commonly estimated from electronegativity. In H–Cl, Cl is more electronegative, so electron density shifts toward Cl, giving Hδ+–Clδ− and a bond-dipole arrow in the chemistry convention toward Cl. A homonuclear H–H bond is nonpolar by symmetry, while H–Cl is polar covalent. Bond polarity is continuous rather than an all-or-nothing label and can change with chemical environment. One polar bond does not make an entire molecule polar because molecular geometry may cause bond-dipole vectors to cancel.
major_error_concepts: Assigning Clδ+ and Hδ− in H–Cl despite chlorine's greater electronegativity.
Treating every covalent bond as either perfectly equal or completely ionic with no continuum.
Claiming any molecule containing one polar bond must have a nonzero molecular dipole.
cards.prompt: Define bond polarity using electron density and electronegativity, analyze H–Cl with partial charges and bond-dipole direction, contrast polar and nonpolar covalent bonds, distinguish bond from molecular polarity, and state the continuum and environment boundaries.
required_concepts: Define bond polarity as unequal sharing of bonding electron density and connect its direction to relative electronegativity.
Assign Hδ+ and Clδ− in H–Cl and point the chemistry bond-dipole arrow toward Cl.
Contrast polar H–Cl with nonpolar homonuclear H–H and treat bond character as a continuum.
Distinguish one bond's polarity from the vector sum that determines molecular polarity and state environmental dependence.

accepted_variants: A molecule is polar when its three-dimensional charge distribution has a nonzero net dipole moment.
Linear CO2 is nonpolar because equal C=O dipoles cancel, while bent H2O is polar because its O–H dipoles do not.
Polar bonds are necessary in many polar molecules but do not guarantee molecular polarity without considering geometry.
cards.definition: **Molecular polarity** is the presence of a nonzero molecular dipole moment from the vector sum of bond dipoles and the full molecular charge distribution in its geometry. CO2 has polar C=O bonds, but its two equal linear bond dipoles cancel, so ideal CO2 has zero permanent dipole. Bent H2O has O–H bond dipoles that do not cancel, giving a nonzero molecular dipole, with the chemistry dipole arrow toward the oxygen side, and contributing to dipole-dipole interactions and water's bulk behavior. Molecular polarity is therefore not the same as having polar bonds. The magnitude depends on actual geometry, conformation, electronic state, and environment and is not a complete predictor of solubility or boiling point by itself.
major_error_concepts: Calling CO2 polar solely because each C=O bond is polar.
Ignoring molecular geometry and adding bond-dipole magnitudes as ordinary scalar numbers.
Treating molecular polarity as the only factor governing solubility, melting, or boiling behavior.
cards.prompt: Define molecular polarity as a vector result of charge distribution and geometry. Contrast linear CO2 with bent H2O, connect microscopic net dipole with intermolecular behavior, distinguish molecular from individual bond polarity, and state geometry, conformation, and medium boundaries.
required_concepts: Define molecular polarity by a nonzero vector sum of the molecule's charge-distribution or bond-dipole contributions in its geometry.
Explain cancellation in linear CO2 despite polar bonds and noncancellation in bent H2O.
Connect a microscopic permanent dipole with intermolecular interactions and possible bulk-property effects.
Distinguish molecular from bond polarity and state geometry, conformation, state, and environment boundaries.

accepted_variants: Dipole moment is the vector measure of separated positive and negative charge; a two-charge magnitude is qr.
One elementary charge separated by 100.0 pm gives 1.602 × 10^-29 C m or 4.803 debye.
Bond and molecular dipoles add as vectors and may cancel even when individual bonds are polar.
cards.definition: The **dipole moment** μ is a vector measure of charge separation. For two point charges ±q separated by distance r, its magnitude is μ = qr; the physical vector points from negative to positive charge, while the common chemistry bond-dipole arrow points toward the electron-rich δ− end and uses a crossed positive tail. For q = e exactly and r = 100.0 pm, μ = (1.602176634 × 10^-19 C)(1.000 × 10^-10 m) = 1.602 × 10^-29 C m = 4.803 D to four significant figures. Molecular dipoles are vector sums over the full charge distribution, so polar bonds can cancel. A measured magnitude does not alone uniquely determine partial charges, separation, or molecular structure.
major_error_concepts: Adding dipole magnitudes without directions when determining a molecular dipole.
Using 100.0 pm as 100.0 m or failing to convert picometers before calculating C m.
Confusing the physics dipole-vector direction with the opposite-pointing chemistry bond-dipole arrow convention.
cards.prompt: Define electric dipole moment as a vector quantity and state the chemistry versus physics direction conventions. For charges ±e, one exact elementary charge each, separated by 100.0 pm, calculate the magnitude in C m and debye using 1 D = 3.33564 × 10^-30 C m. State vector-cancellation and interpretation boundaries.
required_concepts: Define dipole moment as a vector charge-separation measure and state μ = qr for two point charges.
Distinguish the physical vector direction from negative to positive from the chemistry bond-dipole arrow toward δ−.
Calculate 1.602 × 10^-29 C m = 4.803 D for exact charges ±e separated by 100.0 pm and retain four significant figures.
State that molecular moments are vector sums and that one measured magnitude does not uniquely fix charges, separation, or structure.

accepted_variants: Resonance represents one delocalized species with multiple same-connectivity Lewis contributors.
Nitrate has three equivalent contributors and three equivalent N–O bonds in the actual hybrid.
A molecule does not jump among resonance structures; the contributors are drawings of one electronic structure.
cards.definition: **Resonance** uses two or more valid Lewis contributors with the same nuclear connectivity but different placements of π bonds, lone pairs, or formal charges to represent one delocalized electronic structure. Nitrate, NO3−, has three equivalent contributors that place the N=O bond on different oxygens; the real ion is one resonance hybrid with three equivalent N–O bonds of intermediate bond order, not three species rapidly interconverting. Only electrons move between contributor drawings; nuclei do not. Contributors are bookkeeping structures rather than observable molecules, and nonequivalent contributors need not have equal weight. Resonance improves a Lewis model but does not replace a quantum description of delocalized electron density.
major_error_concepts: Treating resonance contributors as separate molecules in rapid equilibrium.
Moving atomic nuclei or changing connectivity when drawing contributors for the same resonance system.
Assuming every valid contributor contributes equally regardless of formal charges, electronegativity, or bonding.
cards.prompt: Define resonance using nitrate as an example, identify what changes and what must remain fixed across contributors, relate the contributors to one delocalized hybrid and equivalent N–O bonds, contrast resonance with rapid structural switching, and state contributor-weight and Lewis-model boundaries.
required_concepts: Define resonance contributors as same-connectivity Lewis structures differing only in electron placement and formal-charge pattern.
Use nitrate's three equivalent contributors to explain three equivalent N–O bonds in one delocalized hybrid.
State that contributors are not real species oscillating in time and that nuclei do not move between drawings.
State that nonequivalent contributors can have unequal weights and that resonance remains a Lewis-model representation of quantum delocalization.

accepted_variants: Formal charge equals neutral valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus half the bonding electrons.
One nitrate contributor assigns +1 to N, 0 to the double-bonded O, and −1 to each single-bonded O, totaling −1.
Formal charge is Lewis bookkeeping and is not the same as an atom's actual partial charge or oxidation number.
cards.definition: **Formal charge** is a Lewis bookkeeping assignment that splits bonding electrons equally: FC = V − (N + B/2), where V is the neutral atom's valence count, N its nonbonding electrons, and B its bonding electrons. In one nitrate contributor, central N has V = 5, N = 0, B = 8, so FC = +1; the double-bonded O has 6 − (4 + 4/2) = 0; each single-bonded O has 6 − (6 + 2/2) = −1. The sum +1 + 0 − 1 − 1 = −1 matches the ion charge.
